title: Mapping Intercellular Protein Trafficking in Glioblastoma with Esterase-Activated Proximity Labeling
text:
Intercellular communication between glioblastoma tumor cells and other cell types hijacks normal brain
signaling pathways, facilitating tumor progression. I propose to develop a novel esterase-activated proximity
labeling approach to systematically profile cell-cell protein trafficking within the glioblastoma tumor
microenvironment. This work will enhance our understanding of gliomagenesis, identify new targets for
intervening in glioblastoma disease, and establish a general discovery platform for studying intercellular
protein translocation in multiple cancer types.

title: The role of oxytocin in modulating activity of the supramammillary nucleus and social recognition memory
text:
The proposed research holds relevance to public health and aligns with the mission of the NIH, as it aims to
enhance our understanding of a novel neural pathway involved in social recognition memory and the impact of
oxytocin on neuronal activity within this pathway. This knowledge will contribute to future studies utilizing animal
models of brain disorders, enabling investigation into whether disruptions in these neural pathways may
contribute to deficits in social behavior. Furthermore, it may help identify potential targets for treatment
interventions.

title: Understanding physiological mechanisms of seasonal reproduction
text:
Lack of nutritional resources, prolonged starvation and cold exposure attenuates the activity of the reproductive
axis in most mammals. This proposal utilizes a multidisciplinary approach to identify neurophysiological
mechanisms of the reproductive axis under extreme negative balance using a mammalian hibernator, the
thirteen-lined ground squirrel, as an animal model. This work will reveal general principles pertaining to the
functionality of the reproductive system in mammals and in the future will provide insight into potential
pharmacological tools related to sustaining fertility in scarce nutrient and environmental conditions.

title: Structure-based functional annotation of microbial genomes
text:
Recent technological leaps have allowed us to obtain the genome sequences of a huge range
of organisms, but our ability to understand the functions of the proteins encoded in those
genomes lags far behind. We will develop high-performance methods to predict protein
structure and function from sequence, and apply these methods to identify the proteins used by
uropathogenic E. coli (the bacteria causing urinary tract infections) to cause disease.

title: Dynamics of the Bacterial Ribosome and Proteome
text:
Contact PD/PI: Williamson, James R.
PROJECT NARRATIVE
This grant application describes broadly based biophysical characterization of bacterial
ribosome assembly. We will investigate the role of assembly factors using cryo-electron
microscopy, both in vitro and in cells, and the ultrastructure of the ribosome assembly locus in
cells using a combination of MINFLUX super-resolution fluorescence microscopy and cryo-
electron tomography. These combined data will develop a comprehensive mechanistic view
of this central feature of bacterial cell physiology.

title: The role of the cohesin complex in hematopoietic transformation and leukemia maintenance
text:
Genetic defects in the cohesin complex member Stag2 are recurrently mutated in various human cancers and
lead to disruption of tissue-specific gene expression through DNA looping. Using cutting-edge epigenomic
techniques, primary patient samples, and a reversible in vivo Stag2 mouse, we will map Stag2-specific chromatin
looping in transcriptional regulation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and functionally assess their
contribution to the lineage fate and self-renewal. Using these techniques in combination with sequential
mutagenesis of the AML driver mutation FLT3ITD, we will determine the effects of altered chromatin structure on
leukemogenesis, the requirement of Stag2 for leukemia maintenance, and the effects on therapeutic response.

title: Multi-Resolution Docking Methods for Electron Microscopy
text:
This project will help biological electron microscopists bridge a broad range of resolution levels, from the
atomic to the living organism. The results of our research in electron microscopy and tomography will be new
computer codes for modeling the structures of macromolecular assemblies. As the basic functional units of
biological cells, macromolecular assemblies furnish targets for drug design because deficiencies in the
assembly architecture are frequently linked to health problems.

title: Genetically engineered mouse model to improve therapy of NUT carcinoma
text:
Successful credentialing and therapeutic development of the NC GEM will provide the global scientific
community with a much-needed animal model that recapitulates the human disease in all important aspects,
thus greatly accelerating NC translational and basic research, ultimately towards a cure.

title: Non-canonical functions of the mitochondrial fission protein Drp1 in ovarian cancer
text:
Ovarian cancer remains one of the deadliest malignancies facing women. Focusing on the mitochondrial fission
protein Drp1, our project investigates the unique interplay between the mitochondria, amino acid metabolism,
and the cytoskeleton and delineates how this contributes to tumor heterogeneity, which is a major driver of
recurrence and therapy resistance. The results from this work will have major impacts on our understanding of
ovarian cancer disease progression and will set the stage for the development of novel therapeutic interventions
targeting ovarian cancer to prevent recurrence.

title: A multiverse analysis of the affect-alcohol use association
text:
The goal of this study is to provide a comprehensive, robust, and generalizable test of multiple theory driven
accounts of how negative and positive affect may be related to alcohol use behaviors. These data will test at
what timescales, for what operationalization of affect and alcohol these associations are relevant, as well as
when, how, and for whom these effects seem to be of greatest importance. This study will improve a
mechanistic understanding of the role of affect in the development of alcohol use disorders.

title: Research Project 4: PFAS Mineralization in Wastewater, Recycled Water, and Water Treatment Residuals
text:
RESEARCH PROJECT 4 (RP4): PROJECT NARRATIVE 
Research Project 4 intends to develop three novel parallel approaches for PFAS mineralization in water, 
wastewater, and waste products from water treatment: microbial defluorination, chemical defluorination, and 
thermal defluorination. Current technologies available for PFAS remediation generally only move PFAS 
from one phase to another, potentially creating downstream environmental problems when concentrated PFAS 
waste streams are disposed. RP4 will result in the development of new methods for PFAS destruction during 
water treatment, so that PFAS contamination can be permanently halted rather than contaminating 
downstream environments.

title: A 3D zebrafish microanatomical and gene expression atlas for disease modeling
text:
The proposed work will lay a firm foundation for an open-access, comprehensive, integrative 2D/3D reference
atlas with gene expression data for zebrafish, enabling researchers to view transcriptomic data in tissue and
organismal context in unprecedented detail. The 3D whole organism annotated atlas will include undistorted
3D histotomography reconstructions across developmental stages that will in turn anchor integrations with 2D
histology that is the gold-standard for tissue phenotyping, including disease diagnostics and spatially-resolved
gene expression analysis. This resource will then serve as a foundation for future translation to other model
organisms and human atlases that can validate, anchor, and advance our understanding of biology, disease,
and development for scientists and educators, ultimately contributing to breakthroughs in scientific discovery
and improvements in human health, biomedical education and public health literacy.

title: Defining intervention targets along pathways from cumulative stress and trauma to alcohol and HIV self-management among young people living with HIV (Project DEFINE)
text: Young people living with HIV (YPLWH) are at high risk for poor HIV self-management, with detectable viral load in 88%, and for hazardous alcohol use which can negatively impact the HIV treatment and prevention cascade. Interventions to improve self-management of both alcohol use and HIV care are critical but have had limited success in part due to the failure to account for developmental characteristics unique to this population and stress and trauma conferred by these characteristics. YPLWH experience higher rates of chronic and complex sources of stress and trauma throughout their lives. Although stress has been linked to alcohol use and disease management, the pathways underlying these links among YPLWH are poorly understood. Evidence suggests several modifiable factors that may play a role in these indirect pathways. Stress has been associated with poor sleep health, which may impact alcohol use and HIV self-management through the effect that poor sleep has on emotion regulation. Behavioral regulation (e.g., decision-making, inhibitory control), is a core component of self-management and may similarly mediate associations between cumulative stress and alcohol use. Consistent with the overall goal of the P01 to improve self-management of alcohol use and HIV care among YPLWH, this project would define developmentally relevant, modifiable intervention targets in causal pathways between cumulative stress and self-management outcomes among YPLWH, most of whom are subject to sources of stress and trauma. Using innovative outreach methods, we will enroll 300 YPLWH age 18-29 to complete surveys of cumulative and intercurrent stress and trauma, sleep health (i.e., survey and ecological momentary analysis [EMA] using an electronic sleep diary), emotion and behavioral regulation, and substance use and HIV outcomes at baseline, 9 and 18 months.

title: Niche Partitioning of Commensal Clostridia in the Gut
text:
The proposed work seeks to characterize the metabolic footprint of commensal Clostridia and investigate how
this contributes to their microbial assembly in the gut. Completion of the proposed work provides fundamental
knowledge about prevalent yet under-characterized human gut commensals and their role in human health and
disease, all of which advance our ability to manipulate the gut microbiota for our benefit.

title: Decoding the dynamics and regulation of parental allelic expression at single-cell resolution
text:
Despite the clear evidence between allelic effects and its influence on genetic architecture and disease risk,
we lack comprehensive understanding of parental genetic inheritance and its regulation during development.
This proposal aims to decode the dynamics and regulation of parental allelic expression at single-cell
resolution, and answer the question that how the allelic imbalance contributes to normal and abnormal
developmental process. It is expected that this data-rich approach will greatly enhance our understanding of
embryonic development, and may serve as an important reference for studying patterns of disease
inheritance.

title: Overcoming resistance to menin patient mutations in leukemia
text:
We are proposing to develop the next generation of small molecules blocking menin WT and menin mutants
identified in AML patients. Ultimately, such compounds are expected to overcome clinical resistance to the
existing menin inhibitors.

title: Project 2: Systems biology analyses of RHCMV/SIV and IL-15 mechanisms of immune programming
text: Project 2 brings a systems biology approach, “systems vaccinology”, to investigate immune response programing by IL-15 and RhCMV/SIV vaccine. Our goal is to define the molecular response by which IL-15 and RhCMV/SIV vaccine program the protection-predictive immune phenotype in whole blood to vaccination, what we term as the “whole blood protection-predictive transcriptomic signature” [wbPPTS] that predicts and underlies vaccine protection from SIV infection. We will conduct three Aims including i) Determine the response to IL-15 in monocytes and T cells; ii) Define the tissue and cell-specific transcriptome correlates of IL-15 signaling linked with RhCMV/SIV vaccination phenotype to program the wbPPTS, and iii) Validate RhCMV/SIV vaccination tissue and wbPPTS signature linkage with protection against SIV challenge. Our research design features in vitro and ex vivo models for analyses of cell signaling/responses to IL-15, and in vivo analyses of cell and tissue application of three "omics" platforms including single cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq and CITEseq), bulk RNAseq, and tissue spatial profiling. Our bioinformatics/computational analyses will integrate functional genomics data sets with immune response and protection phenotypes to determine the molecular and cellular features directing the wbPPTS and vaccine protection. We will conduct bioinformatics of RhCMV/SIV transcriptomic responses in an independent vaccination/SIV challenge cohort to ascertain specific tissue signature of protection and the wbPPTS. This work will be conducted in a collaborative framework conjunction with Cores A-C and Project 1.

title: Empowering Genomics Educators: Scalable and Effective Training Models to Build a Skilled Biomedical Workforce through Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences
text: From identifying pathogenic viruses and aiding in the design of vaccines to identifying solutions for genetic diseases, genomics is an increasingly important tool in modern medicine. To help develop an effective U.S. biomedical workforce, the Genomics Education Partnership (GEP) has trained approximately 24,000 undergraduates over the past 18 years by building collaborative, undergraduate-powered genomics research projects that engage students through Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs). This proposal seeks to enhance the research engagement of GEP faculty and students using short courses, providing training in new genomics/bioinformatics methods, and expanding participation in scientific presentations and publication, invigorating their research engagement to the benefit of all.

title: Partnership in Cancer Research (PCAR)
text:
Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States and Arkansas experiences higher cancer
death rates than the nation. The Partnership in Cancer Research program provides hands-on experiences in
cancer research coupled with education in cancer biology and clinical care to ignite the imagination of future
physicians to solve difficult research problems and improve cancer outcomes.

title: In vivo cell engineering using a bone marrow organoid
text: This project tests a bioinstructive material capable of forming bone and bone marrow in a localized, easily accessible subcutaneous site as a delivery portal for anti-HIV genetic engineering constructs. The larger goal is to enable genetic engineering of blood progenitor and stem cells without requiring hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and without incurring the liabilities of systemically delivered gene modifying vectors. By enabling easy access to a subcutaneous bone marrow organoid, small concentrations of gene engineering vectors can be locally administered reducing the cost of goods and likelihood of modifying other organs. The organoid will be tuned to produce speciﬁc subsets of cells appropriate for the varying anti-HIV constructs in Projects 1 and 2. The ability of this strategy to generate HIV-1 resistant stem and progenitor cells will be tested in humanized mice and non-human primates in close collaboration with investigators in this project and the larger program.
